newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swedish ERM entry seen unlikely soon - economists.
newsitem.headline: Swedish ERM entry seen unlikely soon - economists.

text.p: Swedish Central Bank governor Urban Backstrom has indicated he would favour a link between the crown and the EU's exchange rate mechanism but economists believe an early move is unlikely.

"I always thought that Sweden at some stage wanted to go into the ERM. The question is when, and I don't think it is going to be within the next year," said economist Keld Holm at Lehman Brothers in London.
Ake Gustafsson, economist at Swedbank in Stockholm, took a similar line, saying he saw it being ruled out this year.
"I still think it is unlikely that we'll join the ERM in the near term," he said.

In a recent speech in Stockholm, Backstrom injected new life into fading market speculation about possible ERM membership, listing potential benefits of such a move, even though he reiterated that entry was not topical now.
"I believe that the time is ready to start discussing this issue because Sweden has become an increasingly stable country," Backstrom told Reuters this past weekend in Dublin.

ERM membership could underscore Sweden's increased economic stability and also further demonstrate its determination to continue with a policy aimed at low inflation and sound public finances, he said.

But he said it was important to have public support in Sweden for any decision to join the ERM, which currently groups 10 of the EU's 15 member countries. "We will see how that discussion is developing," Backstrom said.

In an analysis of Backstrom's comments, Swedish bank Nordbanken also took the view that membership of the mechanism, which limits currency fluctuations between the participating currencies, would not happen in 1996.

The bank added that a link of the crown to the ERM was also unlikely before next autumn's party congress of ruling Social Democrats, as developments there could pose a risk to the market's confidence in the crown.

The party is split on whether Sweden should take part in economic and monetary union, and Euro-scepticis may see the ERM as a first step towards joining the planned single currency, which may make it politically controversial, economists say.
If public opinion continued to be strongly against monetary union, ERM membership may even be put off until after the parliamentary elections in 1998, Nordbanken said.

However, others interpreted Backstrom's comments differently, saying they had indeed affected the chances of Swedish membership. "The probability after these comments has increased," said economist Beshara Madi at Morgan Stanley.
A Stockholm-based analyst said Backstrom's remarks had made it clear that the central bank, Riksbanken, favoured ERM entry.
"So it is clear that it affects the probability," he said, adding, however, that he continued to put the chances of membership this year at well below 50 percent.
Economists are split on whether it would be beneficial for Sweden to join the mechanism, in which currencies can trade within bands of plus or minus 15 percent.
These wide bands limit the potential benefits of joining, some economists say, while others believe entry could boost market confidence and help bring bond yields lower.

"The benefit is to lock in the credibility of Swedish policy-making," said Madi at Morgan Stanley, adding that the country had gained much in market credibility over the past two years through its tight fiscal policies.
ERM entry would be "like a signal to the market that there is no way back," Madi said.
